title: The data agreement and privacy notice say our web server only passes requests on, but it keeps each gym's payment keys and payment records
what: The data agreement describes Cloudflare as running the admin app and passing requests to the database, and the privacy notice lists only feedback, help, crash reports and website forms there. In fact our web server also keeps the gym's sealed payment company keys, its UPI ID and payee name, and one record per payment request with the member's id, the amount, the receipt number and whether it was paid.
expected: The legal pages say plainly that the gym's payment connection and every online payment request are kept on our web server, and for how long.
how_often: every gym that connects a payment company or takes a payment online
fix_line: Add the payment keys and payment records to the Cloudflare lines of both pages

title: A look at a gym's payment records straight in our web database leaves no record
what: The data agreement says every look at a gym's records is recorded and shown in the admin app. The gym's payment records and payment connection sit in our small web database, which can be opened in the Cloudflare dashboard. No code writes a record of such a look and no job pulls Cloudflare's own logs.
expected: Either a record of looks at the web database (a job that pulls Cloudflare's logs) or words that say the promise covers the main database only.
how_often: whenever someone opens the web database directly
fix_line: Pull the web database's access log into the support-access record, or narrow the words

title: The WhatsApp "you are verified" reply is always in English, even after the person used the Hinglish page
what: A person on the Hinglish page sends a Hinglish WhatsApp message, but MettleUp's answer ("Your phone number is successfully verified...", or "We could not find your MettleUp code...") is English only. The page language is known when the code is made but is not used for the reply.
expected: The reply comes in the same language the person picked on the page.
who: owners, staff and members who verify a number
fix_line: Keep the page language with the code and send a Hinglish reply

title: The Hinglish WhatsApp message says "wapas jao", a casual form that reads rude to many older gym owners
what: The message the person sends ends with "Yeh bhejne ke baad MettleUp page par wapas jao" (and the same for the app). "Jao" is the familiar form; the rest of the product addresses people politely.
expected: A polite form, for example "wapas jaayein".
who: owners, staff and members on Hinglish

title: Owners are told "The gym server could not be reached", a phrase from inside MettleUp
what: When the sign-in check behind the AI Assistant or the AI column match fails, the owner reads "The gym server could not be reached." The admin app shows this server text as it is. An owner has no idea what the gym server is or whether it is his internet.
expected: Plain words such as "MettleUp could not be reached. Check your internet and try again."
how_often: whenever the database is slow or down

title: A gym owner asking for a demo for the first time can be told he has sent too many demo requests
what: The demo form stops when 300 requests in all arrive in a day (for example during a bot flood). A real owner who has sent none is then told "You have sent too many demo requests today", which blames him and loses the lead.
expected: Words that do not blame the person, such as "We are getting a lot of requests right now. Please try again in a few hours, or WhatsApp us."
who: gym owners on the landing page
how_often: only on a day the shared cap is reached
fix_line: Use different words when the shared cap, not his own, is reached

title: The app file download can land on a GitHub page under the old ForgeAI name instead of the file
what: The download link for phones without Google Play looks up the newest release. When that lookup fails, it sends the person to the general GitHub releases page of the repository named ForgeAI, a developer page with the old brand, instead of the app file.
expected: The link always gives the MettleUp app file, or a MettleUp page that explains what to do.
how_often: when GitHub is slow or the lookup fails
fix_line: Fall back to a MettleUp get-app page, not the GitHub page

title: Once the iPhone app is out, a gym's invite link will send iPhones to the App Store and drop the gym
what: The invite preview says "Tap to join. Gym code X". On Android the link opens the gym page, which keeps the gym. On an iPhone, as soon as the App Store address is set, the link goes straight to the App Store and the gym is lost; the person must find the gym code again after installing.
expected: An iPhone visitor gets the gym page (with its code and a store button), as Android does.
how_often: every invite tap on an iPhone, once the iPhone app is out
fix_line: Show the gym page on iPhones too, with the App Store button
